video_title: Scaling Laws: Public Participation in AI Governance With Hélène Landemore
gist: Democratic theorist Hélène Landemore argues that AI governance is being decided by a small elite (lab CEOs, experts, a few heads of government) and proposes a three-tier process starting with a global public consultation run through the AI labs' own chatbots (reaching ~1B users each for OpenAI and Gemini), followed by human deliberative assemblies and government-backed processes. She ties the public legitimacy deficit to the data-center backlash, possible anti-AI political violence, and a broader push to reform corporate governance (codetermination, shareholder democracy against unaccountable asset managers).

insights.claim: Landemore argues the growing local pushback against data centers is not ignorance of AI's benefits but anger at the concentration of power in Silicon Valley and the prospect of greater wealth inequality, with data centers serving as a visible, physical focal point for that anger.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Data-center siting/permitting opposition is a structural, political risk to AI capex buildouts, not a messaging problem that resolves with better PR.
insights.quote: they're taking data centers as a focal point because it's very real, very visual, very physical and threatening

insights.claim: Landemore contends AI developers will not be able to continue deploying AI (even for goals like curing cancer) against the will of the people, so public involvement is a practical precondition for implementation, not just an ethical nicety.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Social license is a gating factor for AI deployment; watch for labs investing in public-consultation mechanisms as a de-risking move.
insights.quote: you're not going to be able to do it against the will of the people

insights.claim: Landemore critiques Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's argument that labs must win public support by delivering outcomes like curing cancer, saying he picks the least controversial goal while labs are also pursuing contested ones such as job automation and data-center buildout.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Job automation and infrastructure expansion are the politically contested parts of the AI thesis; expect backlash to concentrate there rather than on medical applications.
insights.quote: it's a very easy way to paper over all the other outcomes that you also haven't delivered on

insights.claim: Landemore cites self-driving cars as an example of an AI promise that was declared solved but, in her view, is still neither widespread nor successful, as evidence that tech promises have been exaggerated.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Skepticism of over-promised AI timelines feeds public distrust; a reminder to discount hype-driven deployment timelines.
insights.quote: I'm still waiting for the the self-driving cars

insights.claim: The host notes Dario Amodei publicly acknowledged on X that there is a very negative public perception of AI.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Lab leadership itself recognizes a public-sentiment problem, which raises the odds of regulatory and local political friction.

insights.claim: The host warns that without outlets for popular will on AI, the odds of political violence, upheaval or unrest will grow, and Landemore agrees, citing attacks on Sam Altman as a sign of a populist rebellion in the making.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host) / Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Executive security and physical attacks on AI infrastructure are emerging tail risks for AI companies and data-center operators.
insights.quote: It's it's looking like, you know, a sort of populist rebellion in in the making.

insights.claim: Landemore predicts possible AI terrorist movements that bomb data centers and target CEOs, analogous to the eco-terrorism in Kim Stanley Robinson's 'The Ministry for the Future', and says the Robin Hoods of the future will be anti-AI.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Physical-security and insurance costs for data centers may rise; monitor incidents of sabotage as a sentiment indicator.
insights.quote: AI terrorist movement that has start bombing data center and and taking down uh CEOs

insights.claim: Landemore points to France's yellow vest movement as a precedent where the government only began consulting citizens (the Great National Debate, the Citizens Convention on Climate) after unrest, and argues for consulting the public preemptively on AI.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Historical pattern suggests governments react to AI discontent only after disruptive protest, so policy shifts may come abruptly.

insights.claim: Landemore proposes that AI labs use their chatbots, which reach roughly a billion people each for OpenAI and Gemini, to run a fast global public consultation on AI, bypassing slow governments and the UN as well as national boundaries.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab user bases are being reframed as quasi-public infrastructure, which could invite public-interest obligations on the platforms.
insights.quote: it's a billion people for for OpenAI, a billion people for Gemini

insights.claim: Landemore's three-tier framework runs from (1) a lab-run global consultation through a diversity of models, to (2) global human deliberation such as a global citizens assembly, to (3) local and national government-supported deliberations, and she concedes tier one is not legitimate on its own.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: A framework to watch if labs or the UN adopt consultation mechanisms; tier one would hand labs a new governance role.
insights.quote: that's why the first tier is not sufficiently legitimate on its own

insights.claim: Landemore says labs have already experimented with public input (Meta's community forums on generative AI with Stanford's deliberative democracy lab, OpenAI's democratic inputs to AI, and Anthropic's public-feedback constitution work) but do not go big because the work is not directly monetizable and they lack legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Public-participation efforts at labs are cost centers with limited scale; a legitimizing mandate (e.g., UN or regulation) would be needed to expand them.
insights.quote: maybe because it's not directly uh monetizable uh maybe because they don't feel like they have leg the legitimacy

insights.claim: The host contrasts Anthropic using Claude interviewer to survey 81,000 Claude users on policy topics with Claude's Constitution, which he says was written by a handful of people in an ad hoc, secret process without engaging those users.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Model value-setting is a reputational and governance pressure point for labs; expect calls for participatory model constitutions.
insights.quote: Anthropic used Claude interviewer to produce a report on 81,000 Claude users

insights.claim: Landemore argues the UN is too slow to coordinate AI labs, noting it held one AI meeting in July with the next not until May of the following year, while needing approval across more than 190 countries.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Multilateral AI governance will lag the technology; near-term rules will come from labs, national governments, or ad hoc coalitions.
insights.quote: they had one meeting in in July their next one on AI is in May next year

insights.claim: Landemore argues the very short AGI timelines claimed by documents like AI 2027 are themselves the reason to start with a quick lab-run consultation, since waiting for governments to organize deliberation could be too late.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Short-timeline narratives are driving urgency for nonstandard governance experiments.

insights.claim: Landemore pushes back on the worry that one-on-one chats with a model make people selfish, arguing that on existential issues like AI the link to personal finances is indirect, so people tend to answer in a more disinterested, public-good way.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Relevant for anyone designing AI-mediated polling or preference elicitation.

insights.claim: The host proposes an 'AI deliberation day' on which labs would prompt every user who logs in to engage with a Claude or ChatGPT interviewer on AI governance questions shaped with civil society.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap mechanism labs could adopt to signal legitimacy; watch for announcements of this kind.

insights.claim: Landemore backs Audrey Tang's 'fork the government' approach: build better tools outside existing institutions until governments adopt them, citing Taiwan's 'gov zero' (g0v) and a Finnish civil-society platform that was integrated into government and resolved the gay-marriage issue.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Civic-tech built outside the state can become the government standard; relevant to govtech and civic-AI ventures.
insights.quote: you build uh tools and and and procedures that become so functional and irresistible that even the government then adopts them

insights.claim: Landemore argues AI's stakes exceed the aggregated interests of nations, so governance needs global institutions based on one person, one voice rather than 20th-century nation-based representation that weighs an American life more than a Bangladeshi one.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Ideological push for a global, non-state AI governance layer; low near-term probability but shapes discourse at multilateral forums.
insights.quote: the stakes of AI go beyond the aggregated interests of nations

insights.claim: The host cites Ireland's citizens assembly, made up of one-third legislators and two-thirds members of the public, as a model that increased popular trust in elected representatives.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Hybrid assemblies are a tested template governments could reuse for AI policy.

insights.claim: The 2021 Global Assembly on climate chose 100 citizens at random by geographic coordinates rather than nationality and proposed recognizing a global crime of ecocide; Macron had earlier rejected France's own ecocide proposal as unimplementable because unilateral adoption would make French companies uncompetitive.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Competitiveness arguments block unilateral regulation, which strengthens the case for global standards and applies directly to AI regulation versus China/US competition.
insights.quote: then we will be non-competitive compared to all the companies in the world who are polluting at will and at no cost

insights.claim: Landemore argues international corporations have become more powerful than states and can escape taxation by moving assets, so neither American legislation nor any single nation can constrain them; global standards are needed, as with Exxon and climate.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Signals continued pressure for global minimum standards (tax, AI, climate) aimed at big multinationals.
insights.quote: We we've created these monsters that are more powerful than states

insights.claim: Landemore pushes back on the host's Hobbesian, sanction-first view (via Gillian Hadfield), citing Elinor Ostrom's work to argue that norms set by a coalition of the willing, including AI lab CEOs given a legitimate mandate, can become nearly binding without a global enforcer.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Suggests voluntary lab coalitions and norms, rather than hard global law, as the likely near-term AI governance path.
insights.quote: if we have to count on on some sort of rubies in global leviathan I think we're in deep trouble

insights.claim: Landemore says the labs' profit motive and the extreme competitive pressure from China are a problem for cooperative AI governance that she does not know how to solve.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: US-China competition remains the binding constraint on voluntary AI safety and governance commitments.

insights.claim: Landemore says the next agenda is corporate governance reform, arguing capitalism wrongly bundles free markets with shareholder primacy and the two should be separated in favor of free markets plus multistakeholder governance.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Stakeholder-governance proposals targeted at AI firms could affect control and governance structures of AI companies.
insights.quote: we lump together free markets and uh shareholder primacy

insights.claim: Landemore cites German codetermination (Mitbestimmung), where the workforce holds 50% of board seats, as a model, and stresses it differs from union power because workers act as stakeholders who want the best for the company.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Codetermination is the reference model if labor-board-seat proposals for tech companies gain traction.

insights.claim: Landemore, citing joint work with economist Oliver Hart and colleagues, argues index funds and pension plans are effectively run by unaccountable asset managers who ignore shareholders' pro-social preferences (climate, animal welfare, ethics), even though shareholders would accept slightly lower returns.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Supports pass-through voting and shareholder-preference voting reforms that would weaken large asset managers' stewardship power.
insights.quote: It's ruled by asset managers that are completely unaccountable

insights.claim: The host notes that under Delaware law, contesting a public benefit corporation's drift from its charter requires holding about 2% of shares, so ordinary members of the public cannot enforce PBC missions.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: PBC status at AI labs gives weak external accountability; the mission commitments are mostly enforceable only by large holders.
insights.quote: You have to have like 2% of the shares

insights.claim: The host recounts that one AI lab's internal body for checking that deployments match company values had zero external independent auditors or ombudspersons, justified by meetings being scheduled too quickly for outsiders.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Internal AI-lab governance lacks independent oversight, a likely target for future regulation or investor pressure.

insights.claim: Landemore describes a young Kenyan data labeler who worked for very low pay labeling traumatic content to train ChatGPT-style models, and says global labor surplus means companies face no real pressure to improve conditions because the work can move to India.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Data-labeling labor practices are an ESG and reputational risk for AI supply chains.
insights.quote: if it's not someone in Kenya it will be someone in India

insights.claim: The host cites a Kenyan student noting that 75% of Kenyans are under 35, arguing the youngest likely AI users in the Global South have no voice in AI governance.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Demographics put AI's future user growth in young Global South populations who are absent from governance.
insights.quote: 75% of Kenyans are be below the age of 35

insights.claim: Landemore argues that on uncertain common-good questions, limiting the conversation to experts is dangerous because experts are homogeneous and have blind spots, while including the public costs time but yields real gains in collective intelligence.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: An intellectual basis for pushing AI policy beyond expert-led or lab-led processes.
insights.quote: they have blind spots they they have a way of thinking that tends to be homogeneous

insights.claim: Landemore warns that without public consultation through LLMs now, the result will be the 'tyranny' of Silicon Valley CEOs, a few experts and a few heads of government, which the host illustrates with CEOs getting private meetings with presidents to pitch policy.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: AI policy is currently shaped by elite access; the policy direction can shift quickly with changes in who has access.
insights.quote: what we're going to get is the tyranny of Silicon Valley you know CEOs and a few experts

insights.claim: The host criticizes Congress for going on August recess while, he says, the American public is demanding action on AI, and calls for new institutions that can move at the speed of AI.
insights.speaker: Kevin (host)
insights.so_what: Federal AI legislation remains slow, leaving a vacuum filled by states, labs, and executive action.
